text: You already know the slogan: the provider secures of the cloud, you secure in the cloud. That's true, but it's not specific enough to act on. The real skill at this level is knowing exactly where that line sits for the service in front of you right now, because it moves — and almost every real cloud breach happens on the customer's side of it, not the provider's.

For IaaS — an Azure VM or an EC2 instance — the provider secures the datacenter and the hypervisor, and you own everything above it: guest OS patching, NSGs or security groups, and anything you install. Move to PaaS — Azure SQL Database, App Service, RDS, Lambda — and the provider now patches the OS and manages the engine or runtime. You're left with data, access configuration, and service-level settings. SaaS, like Microsoft 365, pushes the line almost to the top: you're mainly responsible for identity, data, and tenant configuration.

Same provider, same cloud, a completely different job list depending on the service. An Azure VM leaves OS patching and network rules on you. An Azure SQL Database hands the engine to Microsoft but still leaves firewall rules and data access squarely on you. Confusing those two lists is exactly how gaps get left open — or how effort gets wasted duplicating a control the provider already owns.

Look at real incidents and the pattern holds: an exposed S3 bucket, an Azure SQL Database left open to the internet, the 2017 Equifax breach — in every case, the infrastructure the provider secured was never touched. The customer-side configuration was. That single fact is why CIS Benchmarks for Azure and AWS almost entirely test things like Entra ID MFA enforcement, storage account public access, and logging — not the provider's control plane.

So before you deploy anything new, don't guess the boundary from category alone. Identify whether it's IaaS, PaaS, or SaaS as a starting point, then go read that specific service's security baseline — Microsoft Learn publishes one per service, and AWS documents shared responsibility per service too. AWS Lambda's boundary, where you own your code and its IAM execution role, is meaningfully different from EC2's, where you own the entire guest OS, even though both are AWS compute.

That's the model applied correctly: not a fixed split, but a line you re-locate for every service you touch. Next lesson builds directly on this — once you can place that line accurately on one cloud, you'll see why running Azure and AWS together is a multiplier on judgment, not a doubling of raw workload.
